name: Iris Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My alarm goes at quarter past three, which still feels like the middle of the night after fourteen months. I drive an eighteen-tonne fridge truck out of the supermarket's regional depot, two or three store drops a run, chilled and frozen. The best bit is the empty ring road at five with the radio on. The worst bit is reversing into the bay behind the town-centre store, with the bins and the bollards, because I'm still not good at it and everyone watches.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's around you at the depot?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's Marcus, who's been driving thirty years and is our union rep, and he still checks my straps for me without making a big deal of it. The transport office upstairs does the loading plans and the timings. I keep to myself a bit, I eat my sandwich in the cab. My partner Noor works at the city library, so we're on opposite clocks most of the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone at the depot was half expecting robots in the cab by now. I'd post something like, good, now let's talk about the night-shift pay instead of gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays a job, and that's what I wanted. I've got my grandmother's little flat paid off and about eight months of savings, so I'm not scared about money. The thing that would still bug me is the reversing and the early starts, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my runs and finally book the extra reversing lessons Marcus keeps nagging me about, maybe four sessions at the training yard. I'd go to the union branch meetings properly instead of skipping them. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the transport office upstairs. Would anything change for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the planners would get some new software that does the timings a bit faster. That's their business, not mine. I've never even opened the app the company put on the tablet, I just press start trip and go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good year look like for you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good year is I can back into the town-centre bay first time without the store manager waving his arms at me. I'd like to move to the day shift once I've got more hours in. And Noor and I would maybe go away somewhere warm in the summer, with money I've already saved.

say: I'd tell people the **robot hype** was overblown and drivers were right to shrug it off.
I'd push to talk about **night-shift pay** instead of gadgets.
think: My **job stays** safe, and my paid-off flat and **eight months** saved keep me secure.
My real struggle is **reversing** into tight store bays, not computers.
do: Book **four reversing lessons** at the training yard this spring.
Attend the **union branch** meetings instead of skipping them.
Keep putting **savings** aside each month as I already do.
feel: **Relieved** that the job stays as it is, and a little **smug** about it.
S0.quote: I'd like to move to the day shift once I've got more hours in.
fieldNote: Her **security** comes from an inherited flat and steady savings, so money never came up as a worry.
She has **never opened** the company tablet app, which fits her avoidance of new tools.
Her worries are about **skill and confidence**, especially reversing in front of an audience.

steps.text: Book four reversing lessons at the depot's training yard
Go to every monthly union branch meeting with Marcus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what Marcus says, that the bosses always use new tech to squeeze the people at the bottom first. At work I'd tell the planners upstairs to watch out, because their jobs are the ones going. Online I'd share the union posts about keeping a human in every cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the driving's safe for a while but the office stuff isn't. If software does the loading plans and the timings, it'll be timing me too, to the minute, and I hate being watched. I'd also worry that the depot stops taking on new drivers, and I'm the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep saving, maybe push the savings up from three hundred to five hundred a month. I'd ask Marcus to get me onto the union's health and safety course, so I know my rights when they bring in tracking. I won't touch the AI stuff, I'll let the planners deal with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a noise under the cab and you don't know yet if it's serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be timed to the minute. What would that look like on a normal run?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tablet would go red if I'm four minutes slow at the town-centre store, because I took three goes at the reverse. Then I'd get a message from someone I've never met asking why. I'd rather have a planner I can shout at than a screen that just writes it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Janet in the transport office, she's been doing the load plans by hand and by phone for twenty years. If the software does that, she's gone, and she's got a mortgage. The drivers would be fine for a few years, but I'd feel bad going home on time while she's packing her desk.

say: I'd say bosses use new tech to **squeeze workers** at the bottom first.
I'd share union posts about keeping a **human in every cab**.
think: The **driving is safe** for a while, but the office planning work isn't.
Software would **track me** to the minute, and as the newest driver I'd fear **hiring freezes**.
do: Raise monthly **savings** from three hundred to **five hundred**.
Sign up for the union's **health and safety** course before tracking arrives.
Avoid using **AI tools** and leave them to the planners.
feel: **Uneasy**, like hearing a strange noise under the cab.
S1.quote: I'd rather have a planner I can shout at than a screen that just writes it down.
fieldNote: She **sees clearly** that office jobs go before driving jobs in this picture.
Her real fear is **being watched**, more than being replaced.
She shows **solidarity** with an older planner rather than worry for herself.

steps.text: Raise monthly savings from three hundred to five hundred
Take the union's health and safety course on tracking rules
Keep driving the same store runs on the early shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a strong union and the government stepping in, not just the companies deciding. I'd be posting about a law that says no driverless trucks on the road without a person in the seat. At work I'd be telling the younger lads to join the union now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be thirty-one when the robots turn up, and I've got nothing else I'm trained for. The planning upstairs goes in 2028 and the driving goes around 2031, and I'd be in a cab watching it come. I have the flat, so I won't be on the street, but I'd lose the job and the decent pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stop spending on anything big and get my savings up toward a full year. I'd go to every union meeting and the protests if there are any. I don't know what I'd retrain in, because if AI does all the thinking jobs, what's left for someone with no qualifications? Maybe care work, because people would still want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach goes tight just saying 2031 out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking parts of the job change first, and the driving about three years later. What do those three years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those would be weird years. The tablet tells me everything, the office is empty, and I'm basically a pair of hands steering until the robot is ready. I'd use that time to save every penny and to push the union, because after that there's nothing to bargain with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at care work. Would you actually do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, I've never even thought about it until now. My nan was in a care home and the women there were kind, and nobody was going to replace them with a machine. But it's half the pay, and I don't like change, so I'd probably leave it till the last minute, which is my worst habit.

say: I'd say we need a **strong union** and **government rules**, not companies deciding alone.
I'd campaign for a law requiring a **person in the seat** of every truck.
think: I'd be **thirty-one** when robots take driving, with nothing else I'm trained for.
My **paid-off flat** stops me ending up homeless, but I'd still **lose** my pay.
do: Stop **big spending** and build savings toward a **full year**.
Attend every **union meeting** and any protest in the first year.
Look into **care work**, though she'd likely put it off.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a tight stomach at the thought of **2031**.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-one when the robots turn up, and I've got nothing else I'm trained for.
fieldNote: She grasped the **three-year gap** quickly and sees herself as hands waiting for the robot.
Her flat gives a **floor**, but losing the pay still alarms her.
She admits she'd **delay** changing careers, a clear sign of her resistance.

steps.text: Join every union meeting and protest on driverless trucks
Write to her local representative about a person-in-the-cab law
Build savings toward a full year of costs
Put off the summer holiday and any new car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, but with more time to organise. I'd say the union has five years to get a deal on retraining money and a fair notice period. Online I'd share stuff about what happened to the miners and the dock workers, so people take it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots come around 2034, so I'd be thirty-four. That's a bit better, because I'd have my full licence for the big artics and some years in the job. But it still ends the same way for me, and I hate that I can see the robots coming and I still don't really want to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and get my savings up slowly, not in a panic. In the second or third year I'd do the course for the bigger licence anyway, because it pays more while it lasts. I'd keep going to the union and maybe stand as a workplace rep once Marcus retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not as bad. It's more of a weight than a fright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in those five years at the depot, before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I reckon the office goes first, around 2031, and they start trialling self-driving trucks on the motorway runs to the other depots. The store runs, with the tight bays and the shoppers walking behind you, would be last. I might ask to stay on the town-centre runs for that reason, even though I hate that bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stand as a rep. What would you fight for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Notice, first, so nobody finds out from a text message. Then money for retraining that we actually choose, not a two-day online course. And a promise that the oldest drivers get to finish their time first, because they've got the least chance of starting again.

say: I'd say the union has **five years** to win **retraining money** and fair notice.
I'd share stories of **miners and dock workers** so people take it seriously.
think: I'd be **thirty-four** when robots arrive, with more experience behind me.
It ends the same way, and I don't **want to move** even seeing it coming.
do: Keep driving and **grow savings** steadily rather than in a panic.
Take the **bigger licence** course in year two or three for the pay.
Stand as **workplace rep** once the current rep retires.
feel: **Anxious**, more of a steady **weight** than a fright.
S3.quote: I hate that I can see the robots coming and I still don't really want to move.
fieldNote: More warning **softens** her fear but doesn't change her plan to stay put.
She'd shelter on **town-centre runs**, the hardest work for robots, despite hating them.
Her politics show in a clear **list of demands** for any deal.

steps.text: Ask to stay on the town-centre store runs
Do the bigger artic licence course in year two or three
Put a steady amount into savings every month
Stand for workplace union rep when Marcus retires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be thrown on the scrap heap. I'd say the government and the companies have a decade to plan it properly, so if drivers end up broke, that's a choice someone made. I'd be loud about that at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-nine when the robots come, around 2039. That's long enough to have a whole other career, and part of me knows I should. But I'm the kind of person who leaves things, so ten years could just turn into nine and a half years of doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself a deadline, maybe by 2030, to pick something else and start training, probably at the college two evenings a week. Until then I'd keep driving and keep building the savings. I'd keep up the union stuff, because a decade is enough time to win something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but quieter. Some days I wouldn't think about it at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you train in, if you had to pick today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something with my hands where you deal with people, like plumbing or care, because robots in houses feel further off than robots on a motorway. I really don't know. Noor says I'd be a good driving instructor, but who needs one of those in 2039?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd set a deadline. Who would hold you to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor would, she's the organised one, she has a calendar for the calendar. I'd probably ask Marcus too, because he doesn't let anything go. I need someone nagging me, otherwise I'll still be in this cab at thirty-eight wondering where the time went.

say: I'd say a **decade** of warning means nobody should be **thrown away**.
I'd say if drivers end up broke, it's **someone's choice**.
think: I'd be **thirty-nine** when robots come, enough time for a **whole other career**.
I tend to **leave things**, so the decade could slip by unused.
do: Set a **2030 deadline** to choose a new trade and start training.
Study at **college** two evenings a week once a trade is chosen.
Keep driving, saving and doing **union work** until then.
feel: Still **anxious** but quieter, with some days of not thinking about it.
S4.quote: I need someone nagging me, otherwise I'll still be in this cab at thirty-eight wondering where the time went.
fieldNote: She knows a decade is plenty, but **distrusts herself** to use it.
She'd rely on her **partner** and her union rep to push her.
Her pick of **plumbing or care** follows her sense that robots reach homes last.

steps.text: Pick a new trade by 2030, with her partner holding her to it
Take evening classes at the college two nights a week
Push the union for a decade-long transition deal
Keep building savings from the fridge-truck wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd be thirty-one with nothing else I'm trained for and only three years after the planners go. What would help is a law that drivers get proper notice and real retraining money, paid for by the companies that save on our wages. And honestly, someone to nag me into starting early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women who drive. There aren't many of us, and it took me ages to feel I belonged in that yard. Women drivers finally got into this job, and it would be a shame if the robots took the seat just as we arrived.

headlineQuote: Women drivers finally got into this job, and it would be a shame if the robots took the seat just as we arrived.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old** fridge-truck driver for a supermarket depot, fourteen months in and still learning to **reverse**.
She owns her grandmother's **paid-off flat** and has about eight months saved, so money feels safe.
She **avoids new tools**, never opens the company tablet app, and admits she puts off change.
She turns to the **union** and the government in every picture, wanting rules and retraining money.
Her mood moves from **calm** to **alarmed** in the fastest AGI picture, easing with more warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be thirty-one with no other **training** when the robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: A law guaranteeing drivers **proper notice** and **retraining money** paid by the companies.
Someone to **push her** to start a new trade early.
